results.draft_locus: One Order, Three Status Lines ¶4
results.quote: Kestrel & Pine's **Three-Status Order**, #1052877, shows what happens when even one line is flattened
results.finding: Both flow readers re-read here: the section teaches three status lines (money, goods, returns) and the incident named 'Three-Status' concerns one line, its three statuses being three systems' readings of the goods line. The prose never says what the 'three' in the name counts.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 1 (flow reader A, item 9)

results.draft_locus: One Order, Three Status Lines ¶2
results.quote: Shopify's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) keeps three status families on one order
results.finding: Both flow readers understood the dense vendor paragraph only after the 'In plain words' paragraph that follows it, and both proposed the same swap (or moving the vendor paragraph to 'In Practice'). The order claim, vendors, plain words is the one the spec's section flow declares.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2 and reordering a (flow reader A, item 8 and reordering a)

results.draft_locus: The Journey in Thirteen Steps ¶2
results.quote: **steps 10 to 13 exist for every order**, not only the problem ones: at Kestrel & Pine, 24% of items sold online came back in 2026
results.finding: Both flow readers re-read because the evidence seems to contradict the claim: 24% returned is not every order, and Eva later 'did not call'. The draft repeats the spec's wording ('exist for every order') with the spec's statistic, whose declared point is only that the late steps are routine.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 (flow reader A, item 5)

results.draft_locus: The Journey in Thirteen Steps ¶1
results.quote: Pricing, inventory, delivery promise
results.finding: The lead-in says the last column gives 'which system usually has to keep it', but directly after the seven systems were fixed the column names functions (pricing, inventory, tax, search, 'delivery promise' keeping the delivery promise). Both flow readers could not tell whether these are systems, parts of the shop platform or topics.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 4 (flow reader A, item 4)

results.draft_locus: Why the Joins Are Where Things Break ¶2
results.quote: A message can miss those requirements in only four ways
results.finding: After a table with four requirement columns, 'those requirements ... four ways' invites a column-to-way mapping that does not exist; reader B went back to the table and gave up on the mapping, reader A tried the same match (and called it momentary). The prose does not say that the four ways cut across the four requirements.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item 15 (flow reader B, item 7)

results.draft_locus: Why the Joins Are Where Things Break ¶5
results.quote: Two senders, one receiver, no shared record of what had already been done.
results.finding: Both flow readers stopped over whether two different senders each issuing a refund is the same failure as one message arriving twice, which is what 'duplicated' meant so far and what the idempotency definition two paragraphs later covers ('receiving the same message twice'); the AC-3 reader noted the same gap. Neither the spec's p41/p43 nor the prose says why the two refunds count as one repeated message.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 9 (flow reader A, item 16)

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong at Each Step ¶1
results.quote: The four ways apply along the whole journey.
results.finding: Both flow readers stopped at this lead-in because the table does not do what it announces: reader A expected each failure labelled as one of the four ways and found entries that are not message failures; reader B found a column headed 'Step' with seven rows that are not the thirteen steps and had to work out how it differs from the handoff table one section earlier.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 11 (flow reader A, item 18); same passage

results.draft_locus: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶1
results.quote: Vendor documentation and regulation describe the same handoffs with surprising precision.
results.finding: Both flow readers marked this section's place 'partly unclear' for the same reason: vendor documentation was already used as evidence in the status-lines section and in the idempotency paragraph, so they could not tell why those citations sit earlier and these sit here. The earlier placements are the spec's (p20, p43).
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, section note on 'In Practice' (flow reader A, same section note)

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Four Drawings of One Order ¶4
results.quote: **Four drawings, four centers, and not one of them wrong.**
results.finding: Reader A counted three centers and looked back for the fourth: the sentence before says Ruben drew thirty-four boxes and ran out of time, with no center.

results.draft_locus: Eva's Jacket, System by System ¶3
results.quote: Three promises, three sources, and only the price originates in the shop platform.
results.finding: Reader A stopped to work out the distinction: the delivery rule sits in the theme, and the storefront was defined as the shop platform's customer-facing pages, so it too seems to originate in the shop platform.

results.draft_locus: Eva's Jacket, System by System ¶13
results.quote: Wed afternoon, shipped
results.finding: Reader A checked back: the walk says PostNL collected the parcel on Wednesday evening and that such an order leaves with the evening collection, while the table says shipped on Wednesday afternoon.

results.draft_locus: Eva's Jacket, System by System ¶14
results.quote: Six systems, six copies of the order, each correct about its own part.
results.finding: Reader A could not reconcile 'six of the seven will each hold a copy of every order' with a table of five systems, a carrier that 'knew only the parcel' and a returns portal that holds nothing until a return is requested. The count is the spec's (p24a, p37) and is already listed in its open questions.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶3
results.quote: A refusal is an answer within the handoff, not a fifth way for a message to fail.
results.finding: Reader A was sent back to see whether something had been missed: the sentence answers an objection the reader had not raised. The sentence is required by the spec's controlling idea for p47.

results.draft_locus: Why the Joins Are Where Things Break ¶3
results.quote: through the **marketplace connector**
results.finding: Reader B wondered whether it had missed something: after the scene fixed the count at seven systems 'named once for the whole chapter', the marketplace connector and an agency's script appear as further systems in the failure examples. The spec both fixes the cast at seven (p24a) and requires the connector (p39, p40).

results.finding: Reader B could see how idempotency answers 'duplicated' and reconciliation finds 'lost', but not how either deals with 'late' or 'misread', although the takeaways say the two contain all four; the paragraph does not say which way each remedy answers.
